subtitle: "Copy the shared layout recipe and interaction config into your Plotly figures"
jupyter: python3

Copy the recipe below into your own `design.py`, then call
`apply_layout(fig, appearance="light", colors=5, kind="cartesian")` after setting
the figure's title and axes. The recipe remains a **CONVERGING** candidate;
it carries no package installation or stable API commitment. Each figure author
owns data, units, axis ranges, geometry, and scientific meaning.

## Copy the recipe

This section reads the current `outputs/design.py`, so the displayed source and
the executed examples share one authority. `template(appearance, colors=5)` sets
appearance defaults such as colors and typography. `apply_layout` applies those
defaults and controls actual figure layout, returning the same figure.

Choose `appearance="light"` or `"dark"`, and `colors=5`, `10`, or `20`.
The supported layout kinds are `cartesian`, `heatmap`, `three-d`, `diagram`,
`table`, and `pulse`. Set titles and content before applying layout so the recipe
can account for them.

The shared paper backgrounds are `#FAF8F8` and `#161618`; plot backgrounds are
`#FFFFFF` and `#202023`. Title text is 22 px, axis titles 18 px, and ticks and
legends 16 px. Layout uses 16 px outer padding and 15 px axis-title standoff.
Text estimates and native axis `automargin` help allocate consistent padding
around visible ink. Exact figure margins can vary to accommodate legends,
colorbars, and controls. Below a 540 px container width, the ordinary chart toolbar is vertical and
positioned below the title; wider charts retain a horizontal toolbar.
The default legend is horizontal below the plot;
the pulse example uses its container-specific rule described below.

For ordinary plots, the shared layout carries `layout.meta.embla_sizing` with
the base height, estimated legend-item widths, row height, and side margins.
The maintained observer uses the actual container width to estimate wrapped
legend rows and increases figure height by `(rows - 1) * rowHeight`, preserving
space for the plot. Pulse figures use their separate responsive profiles instead.
The same observer handles ordinary plot sizing, pulse layout, and resize/redraw
when hidden 3D panels become visible.

The three categorical sequences follow an indigo-to-red family. Light mode uses
bright purple, cyan, green, yellow, and warm orange-red. The recipe samples linear
RGB interpolation between six reference colors at equal intervals. A sequence
need not include every reference color: the five-color midpoint falls between
green and yellow. See [Colors](outputs/themes.qmd) for swatches and cycling
examples with 7, 12, and 22 curves.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from pathlib import Path

recipe_path = Path("outputs/design.py")
print("```python\n" + recipe_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") + "\n```")
```

## Build and display a figure

This example computes six sine and cosine curves to illustrate appearance.
They are not device measurements. `x` is a phase parameter; sampling is specific
to this plotting example. Switch the page appearance to compare matching figures.

The executed documentation uses `review.display_figure`, a small HTML display
adapter that disables Plotly's MathJax injection and leaves Quarto as the page's
sole math engine. In a standalone notebook or HTML export, use native
`fig.show(config=CONFIG)` or `write_html` as shown below.

```{python}
import math
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import plotly.graph_objects as go

# In this documentation checkout, the recipe lives in outputs/.
# If design.py is beside your notebook, import it directly instead.
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path("outputs").resolve()))
from design import CONFIG, SEQUENCES, apply_layout
from review import display_figure

x = [2 * math.pi * index / 240 for index in range(241)]
series = [
    ("cos(x)", [math.cos(value) for value in x]),
    ("sin(x)", [math.sin(value) for value in x]),
    ("cos(2x)", [math.cos(2 * value) for value in x]),
    ("sin(2x)", [math.sin(2 * value) for value in x]),
    ("cos(x + π/4)", [math.cos(value + math.pi / 4) for value in x]),
    ("sin(x + π/4)", [math.sin(value + math.pi / 4) for value in x]),
]
```

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
for appearance in ("light", "dark"):
    fig = go.Figure()
    for name, values in series:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=values, name=name, mode="lines"))
    fig.update_layout(
        title="Analytical trigonometric curves",
        xaxis_title="Phase parameter x (rad)",
        yaxis_title="Amplitude (dimensionless)",
    )
    apply_layout(fig, appearance, colors=10, kind="cartesian")
    display_figure(fig, config=CONFIG)
```

## Choose a sequence and let it cycle

`colors=5` is the default. Plotly's `colorway` cycles when there are more traces
than colors: traces 6 and 7 of a five-color sequence reuse colors 1 and 2.
For a twenty-color sequence, traces 21 and 22 reuse colors 1 and 2.
Sequence length does not limit trace count or automatically change markers
or line styles.

```{python}
#| eval: false
apply_layout(fig, appearance="light", colors=5, kind="cartesian")
fig.show(config=CONFIG)
apply_layout(fig, appearance="dark", colors=20, kind="cartesian")
fig.show(config=CONFIG)
```

## Keep series colors consistent

`colorway` assigns colors in trace order. For comparisons across figures, assign
named series to explicit positions in a sequence. A paired comparison can use
the same color for one system and solid/dashed lines for two conditions; explain
that mapping in the legend. Here cosine and sine are two illustrative families,
with line styles distinguishing their fundamental and second harmonics.

```{python}
appearance = "light"  # Choose "dark" for a dark presentation.
series_colors = {"Cosine": SEQUENCES[appearance][5][0],
                 "Sine": SEQUENCES[appearance][5][1]}
paired_fig = go.Figure()
for family, function in (("Cosine", math.cos), ("Sine", math.sin)):
    for harmonic, dash in ((1, "solid"), (2, "dash")):
        paired_fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=x, y=[function(harmonic * value) for value in x],
            name=f"{family} · harmonic {harmonic}", mode="lines",
            line={"color": series_colors[family], "dash": dash},
        ))
_ = paired_fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Phase parameter x (rad)",
                             yaxis_title="Amplitude (dimensionless)")
_ = apply_layout(paired_fig, appearance, colors=5, kind="cartesian")
```

## Separate layout from interaction config

`apply_layout` sets figure layout; `CONFIG` contains display and HTML interaction
options. Pass it at each display or export to use consistent toolbar and zoom
behavior. `responsive` adapts the figure to its container; `scrollZoom=False`
prevents wheel scrolling from zooming the chart while reading the page.

```{python}
#| eval: false
paired_fig.show(config=CONFIG)
html = paired_fig.to_html(config=CONFIG, include_plotlyjs=True, full_html=True)
Path("figure.html").write_text(html, encoding="utf-8")
```

## Reuse pulse and Bloch container interactions

These interactions remain **CONVERGING** candidates. `outputs/quantum.py` owns
the pulse and Bloch data, geometry, and animation frames. The shared layout recipe
does not construct these objects. Bring `quantum.py`, `design.py`, and the
maintained JavaScript below into a project when reusing these examples; adapt
the geometry to your model.

For `kind="pulse"`, `apply_layout` serializes
`layout.meta.embla_responsive` with `breakpoint`, `narrow`, and `wide` layouts.
The maintained JavaScript reads those settings and observes the chart container:
below 540 px, the legend is horizontal below the plot and aligned left; at least
540 px, it is vertical on the right. The figure carries its layout settings,
including margins; the observer applies them without separate JavaScript margin
constants. This example uses container width rather than screen width.

Bloch figures carry `layout.meta.embla_kind="bloch"`. Their 65 frames are named
`"0"` through `"64"`, matching the first slider's 65 steps. Playback uses native
`redraw=True`. Reference controls have a light-blue background and dark text,
with `showactive=False` disabling selected-button styling. Each `go.Frame`
contains vector data and `layout=dict(sliders=[dict(active=i)])`, so the same
native frame updates geometry and slider state. When adapting this example,
align `active=i` with your step order and point each step to its named frame.

The JavaScript handles container layout and resize/WebGL redraw when hidden
panels become visible. An immediately invoked function initializes observation;
`MutationObserver` discovers lazily initialized chart panels. Native animation
frames manage the playback slider state.

The following block reads the current `outputs/quantum-view.html`. Removing its
HTML script wrapper makes the same maintained content available to `post_script`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
interaction_source = Path("outputs/quantum-view.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()
script = interaction_source.removeprefix("<script>").removesuffix("</script>").strip()
print("```javascript\n" + script + "\n```")
```

For standalone HTML, use the example figure builders. `write_html` loads Plotly
and completes `Plotly.newPlot` before running `post_script`. The observer recipe
immediately discovers plots, then repeats discovery on relevant DOM changes
and page load.

```{python}
#| eval: false
from pathlib import Path
from quantum import pulse, bloch

interaction_source = Path("outputs/quantum-view.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()
script = interaction_source.removeprefix("<script>").removesuffix("</script>").strip()

for filename, example, kind in (("pulse.html", pulse, "pulse"),
                                ("bloch.html", bloch, "three-d")):
    figure = example(style="reference", dark=True)
    apply_layout(figure, appearance="dark", kind=kind)
    figure.write_html(filename, config=CONFIG, include_plotlyjs=True,
                      full_html=True, post_script=script)
```

This export example does not write extra HTML files during tutorial rendering.
See [Lines](outputs/lines.qmd) and [3D](outputs/three-d.qmd) for the browser-visible
legend and animation behavior.

## Choose layout for the figure type

Use `kind="heatmap"`, `"three-d"`, `"diagram"`, `"table"`, or `"pulse"` for those
figure types; ordinary lines and bars use `"cartesian"`. The figure still owns
camera choice, axis ranges, aspect ratios, shapes, and annotations. See
[3D](outputs/three-d.qmd), [Diagrams](outputs/diagrams.qmd), and
[Lines](outputs/lines.qmd) for complete examples.

Heatmaps of numerical values use a continuous `colorscale`. Categorical
`SEQUENCES` distinguish named series and do not encode numerical magnitude.
Choose the scale, colorbar units, normalization, and numerical range explicitly
for the data.

See Plotly's official [template documentation](https://plotly.com/python/templates/)
and [configuration documentation](https://plotly.com/python/configuration-options/)
for native options.
